cues.text: Let us close this study session with eight independent revision questions written by your tutor.
Treat them as a self-test.
Try to answer each one yourself before I give you the answer, and I will explain the reasoning as we go.
Question one.
What is the relationship between AI, ML and DL?
Think of three nested circles.
Artificial intelligence, or AI, is the broadest circle: any technique that lets machines perform tasks that normally need human intelligence.
Inside it sits machine learning, or ML, where systems learn patterns from data instead of being given every rule.
Inside machine learning sits deep learning, or DL, which uses many-layered neural networks.
So the answer is this: DL is a subset of ML, and ML is a subset of AI.
Every deep learning system is machine learning, and every machine learning system is AI, but the reverse is not true.
Question two.
A model predicts monthly electricity consumption in kilowatt-hours, written kWh.
What learning task is this?
The key is the output.
Electricity consumption in kWh is a continuous number, not a category.
When a supervised model predicts a continuous numerical value, the task is regression.
The answer is regression.
Question three.
A system groups customers without predefined labels.
What type of learning is this?
Notice that nobody has told the system which customer belongs to which group.
There is no labelled answer to learn from.
The system finds structure in the data by itself.
That is unsupervised learning, and the specific task of grouping similar items is clustering.
The answer is unsupervised clustering.
Question four.
A rules-based invoice bot executes repeatable steps.
Must it use AI?
The answer is no; deterministic automation is sufficient.
Deterministic means that the same input always follows the same fixed rules and produces the same output.
If the steps are repeatable and can be written down in advance, the bot does not need to learn from data.
AI becomes relevant when the task involves uncertainty, variation or patterns that cannot easily be written as fixed rules.
Do not assume that every automation is AI.
Question five.
Which V of big data concerns data trustworthiness?
The answer is veracity.
Veracity asks whether the data is accurate, reliable and credible.
Data can be plentiful and arrive quickly, yet still be wrong, biased or incomplete, and decisions built on it would be unsafe.
Question six.
A manager asks why yesterday's deliveries were late.
What kind of analytics is this?
The question is why something happened, so the answer is diagnostic analytics.
Descriptive analytics would only report what happened, such as how many deliveries were late.
Diagnostic analytics digs into causes, for example traffic, vehicle breakdowns or warehouse delays.
Question seven.
A warehouse report groups historical sales by product and region.
What business intelligence capability supports this?
The answer is multidimensional OLAP, or online analytical processing, which is aggregation.
Here the data warehouse holds historical sales, and OLAP lets users summarise and view that data along several dimensions at once, in this case product and region.
This is how analysts roll up, break down and slice figures in a report.
Question eight.
Why monitor model precision and recall, not accuracy alone?
The answer is that class imbalance can hide consequential false positives and negatives.
Class imbalance means one outcome is far more common than the other.
Imagine fraud is rare.
A model that always says there is no fraud could still look highly accurate, yet it would miss every fraudulent case.
Precision tells you how many of the cases the model flagged were truly positive, so it exposes false positives.
Recall tells you how many of the truly positive cases the model found, so it exposes false negatives.
Monitoring both shows costly errors that accuracy alone can conceal.
To recap the eight answers in order: DL is a subset of ML, and ML is a subset of AI.
Predicting kWh is regression.
Grouping without labels is unsupervised clustering.
A rules-based invoice bot does not need AI, because deterministic automation is sufficient.
Trustworthiness is veracity.
Asking why deliveries were late is diagnostic analytics.
Grouping historical sales by product and region is supported by multidimensional OLAP and aggregation.
And we monitor precision and recall because class imbalance can hide consequential false positives and negatives.
